articles.title: The effects of participating in government-led citizens’ assemblies
articles.authors: Mariana C. Duarte, Jorge M. Fernandes, Miguel M. Pereira
articles.abstract: Contemporary democracies face growing public disaffection and mistrust. Governments have tried to revert these trends by promoting participatory governance. Prior studies established how deliberation can empower citizens. However, whether these effects hold in real-life initiatives initiated by partisan governments remains unclear. We test the ability of citizens’ assemblies to foster democratic attitudes in a natural experiment leveraging the random selection of participants to Lisbon’s citizens’ assemblies Participation led to an increase in issue knowledge and salience, external political efficacy and institutional trust. However, it did not impact internal political efficacy nor helped citizens better recognize the challenges of collective decision-making. The results hold for two assembly editions and reveal the potential of government-led participatory initiatives to reconnect citizens with democracy.

articles.title: A harmonized European database of education, telework, labour market and earnings from three Eurostat surveys
articles.abstract: VSET is a harmonized cross-survey profile-space resource documenting the alignment of education, occupation, labour-market, telework, establishment size, and earnings variables from three Eurostat surveys. It combines three Eurostat microdata sources accessed under an approved research proposal: the Adult Education Survey (AES) 2022, the Labour Force Survey (LFS) 2023, and the Structure of Earnings Survey (SES) 2018. The final harmonized database contains data for 22 countries, 1,440,134 unique demographic profile cells, 39 variables, and a summed profile multiplicity of 3,249,634. Occupations are standardized using ISCO-08 at the 2-digit level, educational attainment is harmonized into four ISCED-based groupings, and SES earnings are converted to euros before aggregation. The integration workflow uses sequential outer joins and deterministic coalescing of overlapping variables. The final rows describe harmonized profiles rather than linked individuals. The N_instances variable records the multiplicity of identical rows combined during final profile compression. The release has no integrated survey weight. Its rows represent harmonized profile combinations rather than linked respondents or population units, and the dataset is intended for inspecting category mappings, profile coverage, merge compatibility, and reproducible cross-survey processing rather than for population inference.

articles.title: Affective Authority: Understanding Health and Wellness Influence on Social Media
articles.abstract: Health and wellness content has become increasingly popular on social media. When examining why this content resonates with certain viewers, existing research often turns to concepts of authenticity, credibility, trust, expertise, and authority. In this article, we map out existing work on these concepts across an extensive body of interdisciplinary scholarship within media, communication, and cultural studies, and the anthropology of health, media, and medicine. By analyzing how these theories relate to one another, we offer synthesized definitions of them within the context of digital health content. We then make the case that this existing work too often fails to acknowledge the relationality, mediatedness, and affective qualities associated with health and wellness influencers and their content. To combat this, we offer the theoretical intervention of “affective authority,” which encourages an attunement to how affect, emotions, and feelings emerge through the production and consumption of social media content. We argue that this concept of “affective authority” better illuminates how and why wellness influencers and their content are deemed authoritative arbiters of health-related knowledge.

articles.title: Wise Empathy Improves Well-Being on Instagram
articles.authors: Gregory John Depow, Christopher Oveis, Emily Zohar, Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: Two-thirds of the global population spends significant time browsing social media, making it critical to understand how to improve online experiences to support well-being. Social media use is often linked to both positive and negative psychological outcomes, but interventions to enhance well-being during social media use remain limited. Here, we test whether an intervention embedded in daily life that trains individuals to use wise empathy on Instagram can improve users’ well-being. Drawing from strategic regulation of empathy and wisdom, we used an ecological momentary intervention to train half our sample ( N = 260) to wisely regulate empathy for positive and negative emotions on their own Instagram feeds. Using experience sampling ( N obs . = 5,902), we tracked empathy and well-being in daily life. The intervention increased wise empathy online – boosting appreciative joy, positive emotion sharing and compassion for negative emotions – while reducing negative emotion sharing, upward social comparisons and personal distress. On surveys where participants had recently browsed Instagram, those in the wise empathy condition reported higher well-being than controls, an effect mediated by changes in wise empathy. These findings position wise empathy as a scalable, trainable skill that can enhance well-being on social media by helping users engage more adaptively with emotional content. This work extends our understanding of how empathy predicts well-being and elucidates the relationship between social media use and well-being, with broad societal implications for our increasingly digital society.

articles.title: Like Walking a Tightrope: User-Centric Perspectives on Content in Need of Moderation
articles.authors: Anna Maria Planitzer, Svenja Schäfer, Pia Pachinger, Sophie Lecheler
articles.abstract: Norm-violating content on social media platforms is on the rise, fueling prejudice and polarization. To counter such developments in a timely manner, platforms rely on automated content moderation. The issue, however, is that current understandings of automated moderation are mostly elite-driven, neglecting individual user perspectives, introducing biases and discrimination, and overlooking that users’ perspectives on what constitutes a norm violation in the first place may differ substantially from those of experts and platforms. Therefore, this study uses focus groups to explore what type of content users themselves think is in need of moderation. Findings suggest that users, while acknowledging the importance of moderating polarized topics (e.g., migration) and uncivil discourse styles (e.g., insults), are more concerned with the motivations of perpetrators and the vulnerability of targets. Our findings show that, if platforms want to incorporate user perspectives when designing automated moderation systems, they must move beyond merely detecting problematic message characteristics and focus on more tailored approaches, alongside accountability measures for perpetrators and safety measures for victims.

articles.title: Scrolling for the Truth: Source Factors, Persuasion, and a Test of Misinformation Interventions on TikTok
articles.authors: Brittany N. Shivers Weinstein, Bartosz W. Wojdynski
articles.abstract: The popularity of the video-based social media platform TikTok has rapidly grown in recent years, and with it its role in rapidly disseminating misinformation to its relatively young user base. However, little is known to date about how users perceive misinformation or about how platform interventions could be deployed to stop its spread. Two experiments examined users’ perceptions of TikTok videos making claims about a current health issue (monkeypox). Study 1 tested the impact of information type (true vs. false) and source (journalist vs. influencer) on users’ perceptions of TikTok videos, with party identification as a moderator. Participants rated message credibility and source quality higher for true videos and videos with a journalistic source. Study 2 tested the efficacy of three potential misinformation interventions (a banner label, pre-roll video, and click-through warning) and the role of psychological reactance. There was a main effect of the banner label and public service announcement pre-roll video on perceived message credibility. The interventions had no main effect on source quality, but there was a mediation of the PSA pre-roll and banner label on credibility and quality perceptions through reactance. In both studies, participants had difficulty discerning between true and false claims. Implications for journalists and social media companies are discussed, along with suggestions for future research.

articles.title: Migration and Cities in Chile: Building Territories of Solidarity in Hostile Contexts
articles.authors: María Fernanda Stang, Carolina Stefoni, Aline Bravo, Víctor Félix Da Silva
articles.abstract: This article analyzes practices identified at the territorial level in Antofagasta, a city in northern Chile. These practices have successfully established infrastructures of solidarity between the national and migrant populations, resulting in what we refer to as territories of solidarity. Following Schillinger’s work (2020), we argue that within these territories, experiences of solidarity emerge through contentious processes stemming from daily coexistence in a group of informal settlements (known as campamentos in Chile), mutual support efforts, the creation of alliances, and the production of (counter)spaces and (counter)knowledge. These practices of solidarity take on configurations linked to the organized social fabric in this territory and to the relationships forged with governmental, institutional, and organized actors at different levels. This experience not only emerges and coexists but also suffers and resists hostile migration policies, along with a hegemonic discourse that criminalizes and otherizes migrants.

articles.title: The Supply of Demands: What Black Lives Matter Demanded in 2020
articles.abstract: Despite the significant role social media played in mobilizing Black Lives Matter supporters, political science research on this topic focuses on the years before the massive mobilizations in 2020. This paper draws on a novel dataset of BLM chapters’ tweets during the George Floyd protests to examine the language activists used to facilitate protests during the movement’s peak public support. Despite having more experience mobilizing followers, older chapters were less likely to encourage followers to pursue change through conventional electoral politics even in the midst of a presidential election year. Instead, older chapters were more likely to share educational resources or media that cultivated a collective identity among supporters and followers.

articles.title: Selfish and prosocial individuals both distort their actions’ impact, but selfish distortions can be more contagious
articles.abstract: People often act without knowing exactly how their actions impact others. Here, across nine preregistered online experiments ( N = 8,769 adults, predominantly US residents), we tested whether people exploit this ambiguity to make themselves look good. On average, selfish individuals inflated the social benefit of their choice while downplaying that of the alternative, reporting the two options as more similar than prosocial individuals did (experiment 1a: b = 0.24, 95% confidence interval 0.14–0.34). Prosocial individuals portrayed their choice as comparatively more socially beneficial; they also inflated their implied relative sacrifice, although less consistently. We observed distortions even before people made a choice and when choices were forced, consistent with distortions reflecting social preferences rather than mere justification. While people differed in whether and how they distorted, distortions favouring selfishness showed evidence of contagion: others adopted them and became more selfish (experiment 6, selfish-serving versus no-distortion: b = 0.49, 95% confidence interval 0.10–0.88). These findings offer a psychological foundation for why polarized positions about the social impact of one’s actions may emerge. When social consequences are open to interpretation, people may predictably form divergent interpretations.
